questions.stem: Which enzyme is responsible for the production of hypochlorous acid (HOCl) in neutrophils during oxidative burst?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Myeloperoxidase

 

MPO converts H₂O₂ + Cl⁻ into HOCl, a potent bactericidal agent. It's responsible for the green color of pus due to its heme pigment.

questions.stem: A 17-year-old girl from Punjab is referred for anemia evaluation. She has had progressively worsening fatigue over the months. There is no history of bleeding. She has mild pallor but no jaundice or organomegaly. Her CBC reveals Hb 9.2 g/dL, MCV 68 fL, RBC count ↑ and normal RDW. Her hemoglobin electrophoresis shows HbA2 5.2% and HbF 2.5%. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Beta-thalassemia trait

 

Microcytic anemia with elevated HbA2 is the hallmark of the β-thalassemia trait. Iron deficiency also causes microcytosis but doesn't increase HbA2.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 021-Pathology E&D Part-1, Mission 3.0 (Early Intern Batch) - 25-04-2025 - 2025-04-25
questions.stem: A 19-year-old male from Odisha presents with sudden onset fatigue, mild jaundice, and dark urine. He has no history of recent travel, transfusion, or fever. He mentions eating fava beans two days ago. On examination: he has pallor and mild scleral icterus and there is no splenomegaly. Laboratory investigations reveal Hb 7.8 g/dL, Reticulocyte count ↑, LDH ↑, haptoglobin ↓ and a negative Coombs test. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.label: B
options.text: Acute hemolysis in sickle cell trait

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) G6PD deficiency-related hemolysis

 

The trigger (fava beans), male gender, oxidative hemolysis (Heinz bodies + bite cells), and negative Coombs suggest G6PD deficiency. P/S: numerous bite cells, occasional Heinz bodies seen with a supravital stain

 

Mnemonic: “G6PD = G for G6 beans!”


G6PD → Grains, Glucose oxidants, and Gender (X-linked male)

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 021-Pathology E&D Part-1, Mission 3.0 (Early Intern Batch) - 25-04-2025 - 2025-04-25
questions.stem: A patient presents with mucocutaneous bleeding and prolonged bleeding time. Platelet aggregation studies reveal normal response to ADP, epinephrine, and collagen, but absent response to ristocetin, which does not correct with normal plasma. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Bernard-Soulier syndrome

 

Ristocetin assay does not correct with normal plasma → receptor defect (GP Ib), not vWF deficiency.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. von Willebrand disease: Would correct with normal plasma (provides vWF).

 

Option C. Glanzmann thrombasthenia: ADP & epinephrine response would be absent.

 

Option D. Afibrinogenemia: Fibrinogen affects aggregation, not adhesion.

 

"B for Bernard, Binds Badly to vWF" — GP Ib is the defective receptor → can't bind vWF → no correction with plasma.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 021-Pathology E&D Part-1, Mission 3.0 (Early Intern Batch) - 25-04-2025 - 2025-04-25
questions.stem: A 28-year-old male presents with painless cervical lymphadenopathy, fever, night sweats, and weight loss. A lymph node biopsy reveals Reed-Sternberg cells positive for CD15 and CD30, with a background of lymphocytes, eosinophils, and plasma cells. Which of the following is the most likely subtype of Hodgkin lymphoma in this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Mixed cellularity Hodgkin lymphoma

 

Mixed cellularity HL is characterized by Reed-Sternberg cells in a background of mixed inflammatory cells (lymphocytes, eosinophils, plasma cells) and is often associated with B symptoms.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 021-Pathology E&D Part-1, Mission 3.0 (Early Intern Batch) - 25-04-2025 - 2025-04-25
questions.stem: A 35-year-old male with a history of mild hemophilia A presents with spontaneous hemarthrosis and prolonged bleeding after a minor dental procedure. He was previously well-controlled on factor VIII infusions, but his recent activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) remains prolonged despite factor VIII replacement. Mixing studies are performed, and the aPTT remains prolonged after mixing with normal plasma. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for these findings?

options.label: A
options.text: Factor VIII deficiency due to an acquired somatic mutation

options.label: B
options.text: Development of an autoantibody against factor VIII

options.label: C
options.text: Vitamin K deficiency impairing factor carboxylation

options.label: D
options.text: Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) causing factor consumption

questions.answerText: Development of an autoantibody against factor VIII
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Development of an autoantibody against factor VIII

 

This patient likely developed a factor VIII inhibitor, an alloantibody against exogenous factor VIII, leading to ineffective replacement therapy and a persistently prolonged aPTT even after mixing with normal plasma.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Factor VIII deficiency due to an acquired somatic mutation – Incorrect. Factor VIII deficiency is congenital in hemophilia A, and acquired somatic mutations do not typically cause inhibitor formation.

 

Option C. Vitamin K deficiency impairing factor carboxylation – Incorrect. Vitamin K deficiency affects factors II, VII, IX, and X, but not factor VIII. Also, vitamin K deficiency would not cause aPTT to remain prolonged after mixing studies.

 

Option D. Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) causing factor consumption – Incorrect. DIC causes widespread factor consumption, but it would also show prolonged PT, thrombocytopenia, and schistocytes on peripheral smear, which are not present in this patient.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 021-Pathology E&D Part-1, Mission 3.0 (Early Intern Batch) - 25-04-2025 - 2025-04-25
questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with an enlarged cervical lymph node. Biopsy shows LP ("popcorn") cells with a CD20+ CD30− CD15− BCL6+ phenotype in a nodular background of small lymphocytes. Which of the following best describes the pattern of lymph node involvement in this disease?

options.label: B
options.text: Extranodal involvement with early dissemination to the spleen

options.label: C
options.text: Frequent involvement of mesenteric and Waldeyer's ring lymph nodes

options.label: D
options.text: Localized nodal disease, often without mediastinal involvement

questions.answerText: Localized nodal disease, often without mediastinal involvement
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Localized nodal disease, often without mediastinal involvement

 

Localized nodal disease, often without mediastinal involvement – Correct. NLPHL typically presents as an isolated peripheral lymph node mass and rarely involves the mediastinum.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Contiguous spread through lymphatic chains: Incorrect. Classical Hodgkin lymphoma (CHL) spreads contiguously, but NLPHL does not.

 

Option B. Extranodal involvement with early dissemination to the spleen: Incorrect. NLPHL rarely involves extranodal sites.

 

Option C. Frequent involvement of mesenteric and Waldeyer’s ring lymph nodes: Incorrect. This describes non-Hodgkin lymphomas, not NLPHL.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 021-Pathology E&D Part-1, Mission 3.0 (Early Intern Batch) - 25-04-2025 - 2025-04-25
questions.stem: A 75-year-old man with no history of hemochromatosis undergoes an autopsy after dying of natural causes. His liver and heart exhibit golden-brown perinuclear granules that do not stain with Prussian blue. Which of the following best describes the composition of these granules?

options.label: A
options.text: Hemosiderin derived from iron overload in macrophages

options.label: B
options.text: Oxidized phospholipids and cross-linked proteins from lipid peroxidation

options.label: C
options.text: Retained metabolic intermediates due to lysosomal enzyme deficiency

options.label: D
options.text: Calcium phosphate deposits secondary to dystrophic calcification

questions.answerText: Oxidized phospholipids and cross-linked proteins from lipid peroxidation
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Oxidized phospholipids and cross-linked proteins from lipid peroxidation

 

Lipofuscin is a product of lipid peroxidation, accumulating in aging cells due to oxidative stress.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Hemosiderin derived from iron overload in macrophages: Incorrect. Hemosiderin stains positive with Prussian blue, unlike lipofuscin.

 

Option C. Retained metabolic intermediates due to lysosomal enzyme deficiency: Incorrect. This describes lysosomal storage diseases (e.g., Gaucher, Tay-Sachs).

 

Option D. Calcium phosphate deposits secondary to dystrophic calcification: Incorrect. Dystrophic calcification occurs in damaged tissues (e.g., atherosclerosis, heart valves).

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man with a history of dyslipidemia presents for routine follow-up. Blood samples are collected into several vacutainers, including a red top tube for serum analysis. After centrifugation, the serum is clear, but the patient’s laboratory results show falsely elevated potassium levels. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this finding?

options.label: D
options.text: Use of a red top tube instead of a green top tube

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Hemolysis during blood collection

 

A falsely elevated potassium level is most commonly due to hemolysis during blood collection, which can release intracellular potassium into the serum. This is a common preanalytical error, especially with improper handling of red top tubes.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Prolonged tourniquet application during venipuncture: May cause localized hemoconcentration but not a significant elevation in potassium.

 

Option C. Inadequate fasting before blood draw: Affects glucose and lipid levels, not potassium.

 

Option D. Use of a red top tube instead of a green top tube: Is appropriate for serum analysis, and using a green top tube (heparin) would not prevent this issue.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man presents with fatigue, lymphadenopathy, and splenomegaly. A biopsy reveals monomorphic small lymphocytes surrounding the germinal center in a mantle zone distribution. Immunophenotyping shows CD5+, CD19+, and CD20+ but CD23-. Which of the following is the cell of origin of this condition?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Mantle zone B cell 

 

Mantle cell lymphoma is associated with t(11;14), leading to overexpression of Cyclin D1, which drives uncontrolled G1-to-S phase transition.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man presents with back pain, fatigue, and recurrent bacterial infections. Lab findings show hypercalcemia, anemia, and elevated serum creatinine. Serum protein electrophoresis shows an M-spike. What is the most likely cause of renal failure in this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Cast nephropathy from light chains

 

Multiple myeloma causes renal dysfunction due to light-chain (Bence Jones protein) precipitation, leading to tubular obstruction.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 021-Pathology E&D Part-1, Mission 3.0 (Early Intern Batch) - 25-04-2025 - 2025-04-25
questions.stem: A 45-year-old man presents with painless axillary lymphadenopathy and fever. Lymph node biopsy shows a diffuse large B-cell population positive for CD20 but negative for CD15 and CD30. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma

 

CD20+ without CD15/CD30 suggests a non-Hodgkin B-cell lymphoma, such as Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma (DLBCL).

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 021-Pathology E&D Part-1, Mission 3.0 (Early Intern Batch) - 25-04-2025 - 2025-04-25
questions.stemHtml: A 60-year-old man presents with generalized erythroderma and lymphadenopathy. Peripheral blood smear shows circulating atypical lymphocytes with cerebriform nuclei. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Sezary syndrome

 

Sezary syndrome is the leukemic form of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (Mycosis fungoides), characterized by erythroderma and Sezary cells (cerebriform nuclei) in the blood.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 021-Pathology E&D Part-1, Mission 3.0 (Early Intern Batch) - 25-04-2025 - 2025-04-25
questions.stem: A 72-year-old man with a 5-year history of chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) presents with rapidly enlarging lymph nodes, fever, and night sweats. Peripheral smear shows large, atypical lymphoid cells. A lymph node biopsy reveals diffuse sheets of large B cells with high mitotic activity. What is the most likely underlying molecular transformation?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) p53 mutation

 

This is Richter transformation, where CLL transforms into Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma (DLBCL). The most common molecular driver is p53 mutation.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 021-Pathology E&D Part-1, Mission 3.0 (Early Intern Batch) - 25-04-2025 - 2025-04-25
questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy of Mediterranean descent presents with pallor, mild fatigue, and microcytic anemia. Laboratory findings show: Hemoglobin: 10.5 g/dL, MCV: 70 fL, RBC count: 5.1 million/µL. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Iron deficiency anemia 

 

Iron deficiency anemia Correct. A Mentzer index >13 suggests thalassemia, and the Mediterranean ancestry favors beta-thalassemia minor.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Alpha-thalassemia trait: Alpha-thalassemia trait also has a low Mentzer index, but is less in prevalence than beta-thalassemia 

 

Option C. Beta-thalassemia minor: Beta-thalassemia minor has typically Mentzer index <13 due to decreased RBC production.

 

Option D. Sideroblastic anemia: Sideroblastic anemia has microcytosis but also has ringed sideroblasts on bone marrow biopsy.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 021-Pathology E&D Part-1, Mission 3.0 (Early Intern Batch) - 25-04-2025 - 2025-04-25
questions.stem: Which of the following are seen in iron deficiency anemia? Reduced serum iron levelIncreased transferrin saturationIncreased total iron binding capacityReduced ferritin level
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) 1, 3, 4

 

Iron deficiency anemia (IDA) presents with lowered serum iron levels, decreased transferrin saturation, elevated total iron-binding capacity (TIBC), and diminished ferritin levels.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 021-Pathology E&D Part-1, Mission 3.0 (Early Intern Batch) - 25-04-2025 - 2025-04-25
questions.stem: A 68-year-old male with progressive fatigue and recurrent infections is found to have lymphocytosis on CBC. Peripheral smear shows smudge cells. Flow cytometry reveals a clonal B-cell population expressing CD19, CD5, and CD23. Which of the following cytogenetic findings would be associated with the worst prognosis in this condition?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Deletion 17p13

 

Deletion 17p13 involves the TP53 gene, which is a strong adverse prognostic marker in CLL. These patients respond poorly to chemoimmunotherapy and often require targeted agents (e.g., ibrutinib, venetoclax).

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Trisomy 12 → Intermediate prognosis

 

Option B. Deletion 13q14 → Best prognosis, most favorable marker

 

Option C. Deletion 11q22 → Poor prognosis, but less adverse than del(17p)

 

Memory Aid: "17 is a deadly deletion in CLL”

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 021-Pathology E&D Part-1, Mission 3.0 (Early Intern Batch) - 25-04-2025 - 2025-04-25
questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with chronic liver disease is admitted for gastrointestinal bleeding. Labs reveal: PT: 28 sec, aPTT: 55 sec, INR: 2.6, platelet count: 160,000, fibrinogen: 120 mg/dL. No history of inherited bleeding disorders. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial transfusion therapy?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Fresh Frozen Plasma

 

  • The patient has coagulopathy due to liver dysfunction, leading to deficiency of multiple clotting factors (both intrinsic and extrinsic pathways affected).
  • FFP is the best choice because it replaces all clotting factors.
  • FFP corrects PT, aPTT, and provides volume.
  • Cryopoor plasma or cryosupernatant is plasma from which cryoprecipitate is removed. It is useful for the treatment of TTP or treatment of HUS by plasma exchange.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 021-Pathology E&D Part-1, Mission 3.0 (Early Intern Batch) - 25-04-2025 - 2025-04-25
questions.stem: Which of the following options regarding granulocyte concentrates is/are correct? They are stored at 4°C and can be used up to 5 days after collectionThey contain only neutrophils and no red cells, hence no crossmatching is needed They must be stored at room temperature and transfused within 24 hours They are routinely used in febrile neutropenia responsive to antibiotics
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Only 3

 

Granulocyte concentrates are stored at 20–24°C (room temperature) and must be transfused within 24 hours due to rapid decline in neutrophil function.

 

They are used in life-threatening infections during severe neutropenia, unresponsive to standard antimicrobial therapy.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Incorrect storage temperature; 4°C damages neutrophils, and shelf life is max 24 hrs, not 5 days.

 

Option C. Contains RBC contamination, so ABO compatibility and crossmatching are required.

 

Option D. Used only in severe, refractory infections, not routine febrile neutropenia.



ractory infections, not routine febrile neutropenia.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 021-Pathology E&D Part-1, Mission 3.0 (Early Intern Batch) - 25-04-2025 - 2025-04-25
questions.stem: Which of the following infections is most likely to be transmitted through all blood components, including RBCs, plasma, and platelets, and is NOT reliably inactivated by leukoreduction or pathogen inactivation techniques?

options.label: B
options.text: Human T-cell leukemia virus type I (HTLV-I)

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Plasmodium falciparum

 

  • Plasmodium falciparum is present within RBCs, and can also contaminate platelet and plasma preparations due to breakdown or contamination during processing.
  • Leukoreduction and pathogen inactivation techniques are ineffective in fully eliminating malaria parasites.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Hepatitis C virus (HCV): Primarily plasma-borne, highly sensitive to nucleic acid testing (NAT) and inactivation methods.

 

Option B. Human T-cell leukemia virus type I (HTLV-I): Transmitted via WBCs, and leukoreduction significantly reduces its transmission.

 

Option D. Cytomegalovirus (CMV): Transmitted via leukocytes, and leukoreduced or CMV-seronegative blood is effective at prevention.

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 021-Pathology E&D Part-1, Mission 3.0 (Early Intern Batch) - 25-04-2025 - 2025-04-25
questions.stem: A 45-year-old trauma patient is in hypovolemic shock and requires immediate plasma transfusion before blood grouping is completed. Which of the following plasma types is safest to transfuse in this emergency setting?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) AB plasma

 

Plasma contains antibodies, not antigens.

 

AB plasma lacks anti-A and anti-B antibodies, so it won’t attack any recipient RBCs, regardless of blood group.

 

Therefore, AB plasma is the universal plasma donor, opposite to RBC transfusions (where O⁻ is the universal donor).

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. A plasma: Contains anti-B antibodies, unsafe for B or AB recipients.

 

Option B. O plasma: Contains both anti-A and anti-B antibodies, can hemolyze recipient RBCs.

 

Option C. B plasma: Contains anti-A antibodies, unsafe for A or AB recipients.

 

 “AB plasma = All Blood okay” (Think: "AB has no Antibodies = Best plasma for emergencies")

questions.stem: In the context of Massive Transfusion Protocol (MTP), what is the most commonly recommended ratio of packed red blood cells (PRBCs), fresh frozen plasma (FFP), and platelets to approximate whole blood resuscitation?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) 1:1:1 

 

The 1:1:1 ratio (PRBC : FFP : Platelets) mimics the composition of whole blood. It helps in reducing coagulopathy, thrombocytopenia, and hypovolemia in massive hemorrhage. Massive transfusion is defined as:

 

  • >10 units PRBC in 24 hrs, OR
  • >4 units PRBC in 1 hour, OR
  • Replacement of >50% blood volume in 3 hrs

questions.topic: Cerebellum · 021-Pathology E&D Part-1, Mission 3.0 (Early Intern Batch) - 25-04-2025 - 2025-04-25
questions.stem: A 45-year-old male is undergoing massive transfusion after a road traffic accident. After receiving 10 units of packed RBCs and 6 units of FFP, he develops sudden hypotension and prolonged QT on ECG. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Hypocalcemia due to citrate toxicity

 

Citrate in blood products chelates ionized calcium, leading to hypocalcemia — especially during rapid/massive transfusion.

 

Hypocalcemia → Prolonged QT, hypotension, arrhythmias, and neuromuscular symptoms.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Hyperkalemia: Can occur but causes peaked T waves, not QT prolongation.

 

Option C. Acute hemolytic reaction: Acute hemolysis causes fever, chills, hemoglobinuria—not ECG changes.

 

Option D. Transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI): Causes respiratory distress, not QT prolongation.

 

Memory Aid: “Citrate binds Ca²⁺ → Cold, Collapse, QT elongates”

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why sickled red cells contribute to vaso-occlusion in sickle cell disease?

options.label: A
options.text: They exhibit increased deformability and enhanced nitric oxide release

options.label: B
options.text: They retain a discoid shape and pass easily through capillaries

options.label: C
options.text: They have increased surface area leading to enhanced gas exchange

options.label: D
options.text: They become rigid and adhere to endothelium under low oxygen tension

questions.answerText: They become rigid and adhere to endothelium under low oxygen tension
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) They become rigid and adhere to endothelium under low oxygen tension

 

  • In low oxygen, HbS polymerizes → RBCs sickle → rigid, crescent-shaped cells.
  • These sickled cells block capillaries, adhere to endothelium → vaso-occlusion and ischemia.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. They exhibit increased deformability and enhanced nitric oxide release: Deformability is decreased, not increased.

 

Option B. They retain a discoid shape and pass easily through capillaries: Sickled RBCs lose their biconcave shape and become less flexible.

 

Option C. They have increased surface area leading to enhanced gas exchange: Sickling reduces surface area and impairs gas exchange.
